blocks.x: I'll make a note on here first that we are interviewing Mr. Edgar Joseph. Edgar Joseph. Your address is 1625 St. Philip. And the date is August the 7th, I guess. August 7th. Yeah, August the 7th, 1961. That's right. And this is Bill Russell and Ralph Collins is also here at the interview. Do you mind giving me your full name again? Do you have any middle names?
No, they call me Joseph. My right name is Edgar Joseph.
Edgar Joseph.
That's right.
Do you have a nickname?
Sam they call me for nickname. Sam, yeah. Yeah, this Sam like the nickname they call me.
I wonder if you mind telling just when you were born, what part of the city? I'm born in New Orleans. I'm born 1907.
What is the exact birth date? My name's birthday, be what ever, Alan? You? My name's birthday.
On 1907. Yeah.
What part of the city were you born in? Right here in New Orleans.
In New Orleans. New Orleans on St. Philip Street.
Right here, right along here. Right in the neighborhood, right down there. Yeah.

New Orleans St. Philip. Yeah. That time it was the Rock, it was really a Rock Street around here. A lot of musicians, there came well, there's still a lot of musicians around here. Yeah. That's right. And all.

Eddie Morris, you say, lives right across the street. Right across the street on that side there. I remember when Kid Howard lived there. Howard used to live in H Block down there. Yeah, and Jim and George Lurit. Jim used to live down there, all of them. George Lurit. Yeah. All of them. Yeah. Can you tell us about anyone in your family that ever played music that your father... Yeah, no.
My cousin Pratt, he played with Chris Kelly. My son played with Chris Kelly. He's dead. He played with Chris Kelly. He used to play with Papa Celestine too. And he played with Kid René.
What did he play again?
Banjo. Banjo.
I got a picture, you want to see it? Yeah.
Right on the guitar.
Nice picture. What did you do?
You're a terrible fellow, young man. That's him right there. Oh yeah. Oh yeah.
Wilfred Pratt, they called him.
Wilfred? Wilfred Pratt.

That's him. Yeah. He's a terrible banjo player man. What was that taken, right around here? Right on Roman Street, Rome between Domaine and Sinai. Yeah, he looks kind of familiar to that. Yeah, it's a nice picture. Yeah.
I wonder if we could maybe snap it down there.
Yeah. Yeah. It's a nice picture. Yeah. Yeah.
It's a nice picture. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. It looks like quite a young man there. Yeah. When was this taken about? Oh, that's taken a good while ago. He was a popular man, man. Uh-huh.
Wilfred Pratt. He never really had a chance to get that full independent music.

You can keep talking around. Yeah. You can keep the tape running. Yeah. You say he played with Chris Kelly, wasn't he? Yeah. He played with Chris Kelly. He played with Papa Solstine. He played with Kid René. He used to play with old man Robichaux. Oh, yeah? Yeah, he played with old man Robichaux. Just a, they played the banjo, you see? They played the banjo, you see? Yeah. Yeah. They played guitar? Yeah. Yeah. They played guitar? Banjo, just banjo. Just banjo. Just banjo.
Just banjo.
Just banjo. UStStine.
They played the banjo you said? They played guitar? Yeah. They played guitar?
And banjo, just banjo. He used to play with Guy A. Guy A was the one who shot him. Remember Guy A got killed? Guy A was the one who shot him.
And when was Eddie played with Kelly? About in the 20's?

Oh, it was about the 20's. Right after Kelly died, he laid him out on the sand between Trayvon and Robinson in the middle on that side of the bank. He had a big few of them, Southern Stan. He did? That's right. He must have been very popular. He was. One of the best, he moved a short trumpet like that. He had a short trumpet? Yeah, he had a short one. I had one too, I got rid of it. You know the little small arm like that? I got rid of it. Did he play it too? No, he didn't play it, but he had it. And he's alright, he was a good banjo player. Gotta respect him. He come to John the days when John Morales, you remember John Morales? Yeah. Well that's the time he come up. You know. Did you play with him? I used to go with him. I was just starting out on my horn with him. Oh yeah. And I played around here with Rene, Kid Rene, on the parade. A lot of young men too. Played with Rene, around the parades. I played with Lee Collins, he's there too. Yeah. I worked with Lee Collins, at the La Vida and all. Oh yeah. And Alan Connery, that time he was upstairs with George McCubbin and all that bunch. Alvin Alcon. Oh yeah. Alvin, that's Alvin's brother I used to work with. Oh Alvin's brother, what's his name?
George McCubbin they call him, he's dead. Oh, that's Alvin's brother? Yeah, that's Alvin's brother.
Half brother. Half brother, yeah. Half brother. Now Alvin's right brother.
Well George McCullum, that was the, he was the son of the old George McCullum, wasn't he?
Yeah, that's right. The dad was a trumpet player too. That's the old man, he used to live on Louisiana Avenue, which when he lived there. I'm up there, you know.
No. Well, yeah, there's a lot of confusion there, but there's a junior and a senior.

Well, he got a son now, son and a daughter playing. I know his son is playing. I know his son, Lola, his wife they call her Lola. Nola. That's George McCullum Jr. Yeah, that's right. She had a whole lot of good records too, George. He was a good man. That man couldn't, the only way he played his horn he had to be drunk. He lost about nine horns on street cars. Oh, dear. That's right.
Let's talk a little more about you and get while we're here.
Well, to finish telling you, I got around here with all them old time musicians. I played with, uh...
Were you telling us about, uh, about your, your, any other relations that ever played music? Well, none of my other relations. Not your mother or...
No, my mother didn't know, uh-uh. Not my father. None of my father needed my mother, needed my daddy.
Well, how, how come you started to take off music?
Well, I took it up with old man Shao Ney on St. Gloria.
Oh, yeah?
Had two bits of lessons.
Well...

Well, you come from, you know, come from school sometime. I wasn't there two bits to go play. I lied to my aunt and went to music lessons. Same time I didn't go. He's right there on St. Gloria Street. Old man Shao Ney. He learned white in color too. White in color. He was a good old teacher. See, if I pick up a horn, yeah, I take it. Used to get you like that, Nicky, concert time. One, two, three. Make it sing your notes. First piece of music I learned how to play, when the same go march in the middle of my God today, with him. Oh, yeah. That's why you couldn't play. And you didn't play your horn right away. You didn't get a horn, just make a horn up and play it right away like some people do. Uh-huh. You didn't do that with him. You had to wait till you make your chords, or hum the notes. A, B, C, D, D, G, A, all of that. Oh, yeah. You had hum the notes for him, you understand? You couldn't just say you want to play. One night we was all in there, he sat back in the kitchen. We tried to make, you know, try to play some music in there. All right, really. Uh-uh. They used to call him a pet. Did you get it, Bill? Yes, I think so. Okay, thank you.
What do they call him again?

They used to call him a pet. My pet. Shout him in. Oh, my pet. Yeah, my pet used to call him. What do you get, a little pitch of wine, he'd sit on the side of us and go in there, all right, boys. Get there, get your horn together, take your man and take your knees. Why'd you get it? You know, make your straight leg like that, you know? Oh, yeah. You know, you'd be like this, and it sounds funny. All right. And so, you sit down there by him. You come there wrong, you know what he tell you? Go back home.
And you didn't get to blow your horn at all?

No, you didn't blow no horn right away. You didn't blow no horn until about four or five weeks before you went there. Well, did you take your horn? Yeah, you took a horn. Well, he wouldn't let you play your horn, you understand? He'd make your hum the notes. Like you'd make your sing notes. A, B, C, D, E, R, all that. He'd make you sing all that. Uh-huh. Yeah, and a singer humming with him.
But you didn't take your case at your horn?

Yeah, I had my case right there with your good night. I'd take that one out and play nothing. You couldn't take it out? No. He'd take the time and he'd make you sit down there and he'd ask you questions. And now he'd ask you how many notes in music and how you divide the music. What are seven notes in music? In other words, four notes. You understand? You can make more than that. He'd ask you all them questions like that. Well, sometimes you wouldn't have your mind. He kept you on a snap journey to catch you sometimes. You understand what I mean? Yeah. Well, he'd know why he'd catch you. He'd know you ain't been doing stuff in your horn. Yeah. And after you get there, you get there, you go home, man, get home, clap, blow, blow, blow. He'd know a little old scale out for the mirror of my guard today. You know, the voice piece of music you play with. You go home, bam, Man, you learn that? Man, it's always the highest thing in the world after you learn that through the beastly. So, come back to you say, well, I'm going to try. You see, can you play this? You think you're going to play something? You make all the boys get their horn. About six of us. Get your horn. Guess what he'd put on you? On the sink, go marching in. Don't, don't, don't, don't. Clannets, trumpets. He'd have all that cleats. Clannets, trumpets, bass drum, violin. All students. All students. All students, right there in the house. All bunch of youngsters. Can you remember who else was studying with you at that time? Gilbert Young was, Gilbert was going there too. You know Gilbert Young? Yeah. Wake up at the, at the post office. Gilbert, well Gilbert used to be the worst one in the bunch. Oh, man, I troubled Gilbert. See his son Gilbert to take, you know what he'd do, Bill? Gilbert would spend his money. That time Gilbert was living none, yeah. Gilbert used to be, you know, like all kids. Yeah. Gilbert would go to the show. I ain't lie, I was going to the show too. I went to the show too. Take the horn, go in the show, come back, you all, they went to the lesson. At the same time I'd be lying, I was lying. I ain't even say I didn't lie, I didn't lie too. We used to do that. So, we got into him, said let's make up my mind. This man, we might have to go ahead. Well, he was the only one lying you could pay two bits of lesson. See, that other fella was charging a dollar and something. That time they had a fella in the other time they called a fair boss. He was charging a dollar and something to go get lessons. And they had a Monetta across the river, you know Fess. Well, Fess was charging kind of high, because Fess had a lot of them white boys across the river. Well, we couldn't fool Fess, that was too much. And I'll tell you another story I took and done. Now I learned how to get my horn really good. I got around them old mans. So, I say to myself, I'm going to do something with this horn right now. I get all them old time musicians. I even got with Shabbs. You know Shabbs was a good trumpet player. Yeah, I heard it. Right behind Lewis. So, one Sunday shot, called me up and said, I got a prayer. I'll never forget a jolly boy prayer. Think he can make it? He said, yeah, I can make it. Man, I knew if I could make it. I went just the same. I went with Shabbs. Man, I done one of them. So, after, come in and get there. Man, I might have, boy, you making a whole lot of noise. That time I had that little short trumpet like that. Burn that, burn that, son. Yeah. And while I was doing trinchement work, I find horn and I passed the horn up myself. I passed the horn up. Sheep would tell you the same thing. Sheep had an old horn too. I'll tell you about this. Same time, when that thing's on story, that, sheep had old horn, it was patched. It was all bent up. Well, I took the horn apart. I was doing metal work. I could do it good. I fixed the horn up. He had learned the horn to kick Howard. What Howard took and done. Howard took and, see, after I fixed the horn for sheep, Howard took the horn. Sheep come out his horn from Howard. Howard had a job to go play at night. She'd tell you about that. So, him and Howard had it. So, I said, sheep, Howard, I learned you my horn. I learned you my horn. What Howard was good to, you understand? Well, Howard had done good to watch me too. Howard was hiring me too. So, the only one that asked him, thing back. I turned around there. I goes on a, this is my cousin. I goes with, with a lamb. You remember lamb? You spread the old record? He gets the old, the old, the old noise. You know the old noise uptown. I think. So, I called him. But, they like, corn. Lamb said, you want to make, you want to make a couple of hours? Yeah, I'm making. Man, I started with lamb. Round about 11.30. Man, my lift got so weak. And I thought to come on home. I told lamb, I can't make it no more. I said, don't be scared, boy. Don't be scared. So, man, I took him. You know, drink maybe by drinking. And maybe, you want me to come up and bat him. So, I said, 12 o'clock. We was up around, uh, Louisiana. You know where they make the tongue come down, St. Charles. I said, sheep, they ain't no use me going to myself. I said, they ain't no use me going back home. I ain't got to St. Charles. And St. Charles and Louisiana. I said, I said, I'm going to put it in the good Lord's hand. I'm going to try to make it. And, man, do you know I made it? I made it. I come all the way down to Canal Street. That time, we had to go to Canal Street and come back up and walk it. Long way. Long way. Well, we made a stop on Magazine. Somewhere around St. George Street, there's the feeders up there, you know. They give us something neat. So, lamb said, you know how you feel better now, boy? I said, yeah, man, I felt good. When they hit the Poirier Avenue, going out towards South Street, you understand? I felt more better, you understand what I mean? When they hit the way up around Nashville. Man, I can make another one like that again tomorrow. Make another one like that. That's how I begin to make myself. You understand what I'm doing? So, after another boy, I started playing with George E. Parker at the Happy Landing. Tell you. See me, I had plenty of knowledge. So, at night, the Union had was 12 fans at the Jitsa T-Room. Jitsa T-Room. With George E. Parker, I played with George E. Parker. I had me, George E. Parker, Michael Lee. Uh, his boy played guitar. I know you didn't hear about him. He drives a lumber truck. The lumber truck. The lumber truck.

back in town, Ruben, Ruben they called him. Ruben, Ruben can tell you. Well we had about nine pieces and Dave, well Dave Band was up there too playing. And so Dave, uh, Dave was telling me. So I'm gonna tell you man, I got up there, Mike I swear to Jesus Christ boy, there was there and Bigfoot Billy was with it. Stay down there, I'm trying to never man you sure be asking me that. So Mike, Mike seen Dave with Dave Band, Dave played a couple of them. Man he said no lie Mike, I'm not lying. Mike in California, Mike packed up his home and said man I ain't trying to get that band. I said what's the matter? I said you're getting paid like it but. Man I know where I got the strength at. In the same building I got up and I got against Dave. Me and Dave had it. So people come up there, so Mike, a little museum come out and I said, I didn't know you could do that. I said many things I can do, I can't do, I tried myself in doing it, playing music, you understand what I mean? So that got all right. Well after we finished, the youths had come all, all band had to play about three hours to play. And the way the union was funded the music to build money for the union, you understand what I mean? But the union wasn't like it is, nah. The union didn't have the money like they got not, you understand me? So we turned around there, we turned around, I get the job at the Masonic Temple on St. Charles on the 14th floor up there. I played up there for some American Can Company, some big shot of the American Can Company. They got a beautiful stand, I don't know if you ever been up there and seen them stand, they got up there. We played up there, who they had up there, they had Rush for the player union and Tony Ambricko. Oh yeah. Three bands up there. Nah, you know, I had some boys with it, I had some boys with
them bands, man, you could let them, look at them in the stores there. Man, you worried about them, man, they come up here to make money. We

make them. We made it on that. Time around from that, they hired me. I played the world convention, I wish I had that picture to show you. I had a book of me. The whole village, I tell you who was playing with me. Boy was like Dr. Cleo, you remember Cleo, you played bass? Oh yeah. You played with Howard. I had Cleo, you remember Tato. Oh yeah. Point out playing with me. Alto. Alto, yeah. I had his brother on piano and had a boy that called Paul Antwine and Harmon Antwine. We played at the world convention. Tony Ambricko was downstead and we was upstairs. While we played, ma'am. Ma'am. If you want to stop anytime, go ahead. No, wait, I was in Valorant. In the finish time we leave there, we leave off the, new ferry boat, we go to New Orleans Airport and play it again. We played that night that day. So then boys, you know what people doing, I just wish I had the book to show you. You know what I'm doing? Cleo, man, they bought us everything. They took all kinds of pictures of us. Cleo was riding the bass. You know Cleo used to take and ride that bass and play it like that. And well, made it on that. I made it on that turnaround. I get another job, same company I work for, the Acme Insurance Company. I played at the Junk Hotel for them. Well, everywhere I went, they had white bands. And that's what gave me courage to bring me up on, not to be scared to play my horn with nobody. See? You got sellers that's playing, you know they see another band, they get scared. But I'm not scared of nobody. If a man's better than me, that's what I was thinking. You understand what I mean? I take it like that. If you better than me, I ain't gonna say nothing. Well, someday I might catch up with you. You understand what I mean? I might catch up with you. I don't say I'm no star. You understand what I mean? Well, I'm gonna do my part when I'm supposed to do. And right now the band I got. I got a band. I got a good set up of boys. I ain't got no youngsters. I'll tell you what I got. I use Bigfoot Billy. I use Charlie Anthony. Charlie Hamilton. Yeah, piano player. Play piano with me. I use Homer Lejean. He plays great guitar and trombone. When Clem is not playing at the Paradise, I use them on bass with me. That's the kind of band I'm doing. And don't you think them old man can't play? Them old man really plays some music. You understand what I mean? Sure. What I like about them, them young, them youngsters is alright. But they don't know nothing to beat them old man. See now, like we got a dance at the Auto Crack Out Club, the Lions Club. What we got down now, see they got a big 14 band, 14 piece band. All you can sign. See it's 14 piece of music. I take six pieces and
run them in the river with it. That's right. What do you think makes the difference between the young man and the old man?

What do you think makes the difference? I think the old man know what they're doing better than the youngsters. The youngsters, you see the youngsters, they take and they want to do, they want to do too many things. It's only one thing you can do when you're playing music. Sit down and try to play a straight lead and play your horn right. With all that monkey shine, you don't be doing that. See them jumping off the bandstand with a horn in your mind, enough for you to fall off a stadium and cripple yourself with that. You know it yourself. I know a bunch of them white boys, they don't do that. They play the horn like they're like the color sound and play like they're supposed to play it. You understand what I mean? Sound played like that. Where you gonna get to jumping and all that and throwing, jumping off a chair? You don't be doing that. Right. You don't play music putting on a show. That's right. That's what they call putting on a show. But that still, not playing your horn like they're supposed to be playing. See? Now, I look at some of them fellas. I got fellas with me. See them fellas, they can play and they know what they're doing. They never catch them crying. They don't play the part where they're supposed to play. See? Now you see at Andrew Higgins' house. I used to play up there too, up on Patanian Street. You know Patanian stuff It was a corner, we played for them. I played a whole lot of crowd, doing big dances for them. And the holidays, you understand me Bill? Well they had three of us, wonderful. Of course, and I played for them people, and I played for them people. I didn't make no price with them. I supposed to get off at 2, you know what time I got off? 6 o'clock in the morning. Said just go ahead and play, whatever it is, I'll make up the difference. Now they got a white fella, Mr. Wagman, right behind the country club. Nobody knew him at the country club. Country club's on that side, you got a house on that side. Well every year I played his daughter, Devil Jude, dance. Well we don't start till around quarter to 10. Well that dance lasts till 6, 7 o'clock in each morning. That's the kind of jobs I get with them kind of people. And the people that are playing for them people, they never ask you nothing. You understand what I mean Bill? All they want you is give them respect and kind, and give them the music that they want to. When they start drinking and they want to dance, you got to just feel like they want to dance. You understand, you can't just stop, get tired and say well, we take an intermission. When we start late like that, we don't take any intermission. We run for them to tell us to relax a while, let them rest, and we go to playing again. That's how we get along with the people. That's how I get all my gear with the people. And anywhere I went, I would try to satisfy anybody. Now, about a week ago we played up here on the Poison Avenue. I know if y'all have been in there, a Jewish club. Up on the Poison Avenue? It's between Magazine and 8th Street and the Miller Block. They got a beautiful hall. You been in there?
No, I don't think so.

It's a beautiful place. All air conditioning in there. They got around about 500 some more tables. I know the Acme Insurance Company is fixing to give their Christmas party up there. I told them about a place. They asked me where they think they'd be able to get a place. And I would charge my band. I told them what I asked them. Well, for them, I charge them $135 for seven pieces of music. That's a Christmas party. Now, every year, I played by Miss Commander. You ever been there? No.
You ever been there?
No, I haven't been there either. In Washington Avenue? Yeah, I know the place.
It's a big gift.

She can tell you what. I played all the dances every Christmas for them. Every year. She got something, man. I swear y'all will see. You ever see heat in it? You know how cold it is last year? How cold it is? Yeah. She got in the yard. They got lights, heat in the yard. It's like summertime. Yeah, man.
That's right.

You see they come over like this. Cover it over. No, they don't cover it over. It's like this. About this wide. Say about three inches wide. You understand what I mean? They got gas lights in them. Oh, yeah. Oh, man. That thing be so warm. The same billy can tell you. The only boy that's trying to happen to tell you. They had Darcy with me on the beach up there. Oh, yeah. And, man, it was so hot in that yard. And it was freezing outside. It was really freezing out there.
That's the first time I've ever seen anything like that. Yeah. First time I've ever seen anything like that.

Well, I mean, last time we finished, she said, we couldn't play out in the yard. But this year, she said, we can give you all that yard. We didn't play upstairs. They got a beautiful dance hall upstairs. She said, Mr. Maher, they called him this morning. And Mr. Commander, he can tell you about me, Mr. Adam, Mr. Joseph. Every year I get that job. Sign a contract. Every year. Nobody else. But I used seven pieces with them. He's very nice. And, man, he got something there. I've never seen nothing like that in my life. You see how that guy's been heat like heat work in the yard when it's open.
Yeah, that's really something.

I wish it, next year, my gosh family, next year, when I play out there, I'm in trouble. When I play out there, I'm going to try to get in touch with y'all and let y'all come up there and make a picture.
Yeah, I'd like to see that.
I'd like you to see that. I'd like you to see that, see how that thing, how the heat gets there. You can come in there. I've seen some pictures of the inside.
Inside. Of the place.

Well, he wins the prize every year on the best Christmas lights. You think he must cost him money? He gets them big, you know them big cranes that put them lights, neon lights all night? He put them cranes to put them lights in. It's beautiful to see what he has signs and all that. You understand me? Well, nothing to catch on fire. Next time I'm in there, they say, God spare me from living. I'm going to get in touch with y'all and have y'all come up there. Christmas fall on Sunday, whatever it's fall on, I'll let you know and y'all come up there. Y'all going to be my guests until y'all know I'm going to have some guests come up there. All right. I even had the priestess dancing up there. Cali priests, well they come to me. They ask me a question, cause I'm Cali too, you see? And I belong to 90 feet of Cleveland. We got a place on Arlene Street. We just come in there shut my hand. He said, Joseph? I don't dance, but I'm dancing this music. You know what he danced with? He made us do. He got there and made a parade out of it. We played the Saints Go Marching and I had Eddie Johnson with me. Worked by Worldline, you know Eddie Johnson. Yeah, that's Eddie. He made us march all to the border. And guess who was the grand march? The priest. The priest and some lady's with me. And man, you're a fella I haven't seen that man the priest. And nobody all night they love. Going around there. I said look at her and she's jessing now. I said what? Man, y'all wish y'all have been there where you could snap a picture of that. Man, you would love to see something like that.
Do you understand me?
That's the first time I ever seen anything like that.
Well I guess that's just made him feel good. That's right.

You'd be surprised when you do some people. You know what he told me? He told me, he said, well I just come in Joseph. He's from New York. He said, I've been around places. When I never seen a place Mr. Commander got us to play. When the same girl watched his name find him about nine times. So then Mr. Moran told him, he's gonna show him how he makes the carnival parades down there. Well all the guests, white girls and white boys, they're all in applause. They got the girlfriend man, watching her on. And we playing watching with him. Man, that was something good to see. So now I didn't see something like that. That was really good. They have nice parties. Now, other thing I had played on these little appetizers. Nice to play every Sunday for the Hawks at the center centers. Where they have a dance. Nice to play the appetizers too. When was that? How long ago was that? Oh that's a good while ago. That's about three months ago. Oh three months ago. Three months ago. That time we used to have bands and trucks. Do you understand what I mean?
Well I remember too.
About six pieces riding on the truck. You see they go around riding in cars.
You did that just three months ago? Yeah, yeah. Oh I didn't know.
Do that, going around different places like that. And appetizing. You understand for the dance. You were on the truck? Yeah. On your band?
No.

We used six pieces like that. Six pieces. Six pieces. We ride around the truck. Go maybe uptown. We leave from uptown. We come down to Burgundy. And when we coming in. Going to the center center. Well we start the plane from Yale. Playing either the same group marching in. With the truck going slow. And they make like a parade. The boys get out the automobile. They get to put their car and they march. And they march to the center center. It's like a parade. Oh you're riding the hall.
Yeah.

They make a parade out of it. You'd be surprised how much cake that is. What a truck be going slow. At the same time. You understand what I mean? Yeah. And man it. Billy do me so good sometimes. When I. See them boys having fun like that. Sure. Sometimes I'm sorry when it's over.
Yeah.

You know what? I be enjoying myself. Sure. I be enjoying myself. Just like it's me down there. Go see we in the working. And all them boys in the band they like that too. Yeah. See that makes. That makes. That's what makes a band.
Makes people happy.

Makes people happy. And makes people happy and that makes you a band. It's the best thing in the world to be with a bunch of men. Everybody agreed in one thing. And then. I'm going to play. I'm going to play. I'm going to play.
But if you got contrarian fellas in the band, you never have a band. See?
